Unless selected, this transfer will be OUTRIGHT without a retained interest.{[elseif peek(DeedState != "Louisiana")]} may be required to maintain the homestead exemption and /or any available "senior freeze" with respect to a Principal Residence in {[peek(DeedState.Name)]}. Unless selected, this transfer will be OUTRIGHT without a retained interest.{[endif]}{[else]}This transfer will be subject to a retained {[if peek(DeedState == "Louisiana")]}usufruct{[else]}life estate{[endif]} in favor of the Transferor(s), which will maintain the homestead exemption and "senior freeze" in Louisiana. This may NOT be required in other states for homestead exemption purposes.{[endif]}.

CAUTION: A Notarial Act of Correction may only be used for clerical errors, such as typographical errors. Substantive errors require the joinder of all parties to the original Act of Transfer/Sale/Donation.

###
Legal Description
The Act of Donation must include a full and complete legal description; note that the abbreviated legal description, such as the one that normally appears on your tax assessor notice, is not sufficient. The full legal description can be found in the deed, act of sale, judgment of possession, act of donation, or other conveyance document for your home. If you don't know the legal description, answer "No" below and you can add the legal description to your documents once you receive them.

properties.name: WarrantyType
properties.label: Select the **Warranty of Title** to be provided by the Transferor.
properties.helpText:
GENERAL WARRANTY DEED:
A general warranty deed provides the highest level of protection to the buyer, guaranteeing against title defects and third-party claims from the property's entire history, even those that existed before the current seller owned the property. This type of deed includes six specific covenants that the grantor makes to the grantee. These covenants cover the grantor's ownership and right to sell, the absence of undisclosed encumbrances, the buyer's quiet enjoyment of the property, the grantor's promise to defend the title forever, and the grantor's commitment to take future actions if needed to perfect the title. 

SPECIAL WARRANTY DEED:
A special warranty deed offers more limited protection compared to a general warranty deed. The grantor only guarantees against title issues or encumbrances that arose during their period of ownership. This means the grantor is only responsible for issues caused by their own actions or omissions while they held the property. Special warranty deeds are often used in situations where the grantor hasn't owned the property for a long time, such as in bank sales or foreclosures. 

QUITCLAIM DEED:
It's also important to understand quitclaim deeds, which are different because they do not offer any warranty of title. With a quitclaim deed, the grantor simply transfers whatever interest they may have in the property, without making any guarantees about the title's validity or whether any claims exist. These deeds are typically used in specific situations, such as transfers between family members or in divorce settlements, where the parties involved have a high level of trust and the risk of title issues is accepted by the grantee.
